930.bp: Online stores want to predict whether a shopper will buy something, so they can show better deals or personalized product pages to the right people at the right moment. The better the prediction, the more revenue the store makes.
930.wh: The hard part is that different customers behave in completely different ways. A typical prediction model uses the same mathematical rules for everyone, which misses how unique each customer's decision-making actually is. Traditional approaches also try to use the same features to both understand the customer and to adjust how the model works, which creates competing demands in the math—like trying to serve two masters with one rule.
930.ap: This paper proposes APPNet, which splits features into two buckets. One bucket feeds into the main prediction model (the part that decides buy or no-buy), and the other bucket tells the system how to personalize that prediction model for each customer. Instead of hand-picking which features do what (which requires human guessing), the system learns automatically during training which features should go in which bucket by watching where the math goes wrong.
930.ww: By separating the features, you avoid the tug-of-war—each bucket can do its job without fighting the other. Letting the system figure out the split automatically, rather than guessing ahead of time, means it discovers which features actually predict customer types and which predict whether they'll buy. This way, each customer gets rules tailored to them.
930.po: The paper shows this system predicts purchases better than models that treat all customers the same, and better than older personalization methods that guessed which features to use for grouping.

931.bp: Training machine learning models needs lots of labeled examples (like 'this email is spam' or 'this image is a cat'), but creating that data by hand is slow and expensive. Scientists use large language models to generate fake data to use for training instead.
931.wh: Most people have been doing this backwards without realizing it. The natural order is: first generate diverse examples of things (emails, articles, images), then label what they are. But most researchers put the label in the prompt first ('generate a spam email'), which forces the model to work backwards from the label to make matching data. This reversal might create data that's systematically different from real-world examples.
931.ap: This paper tests both directions. They use the same language model to create synthetic datasets two ways: the natural way (generate first, then label), and the popular way (label first, then generate). They then train two types of models on each synthetic dataset and test against real human-labeled data to see which approach gives better performance.
931.ww: When you generate first then label, the model creates natural diversity and the labels come later as honest descriptions, mimicking how real data arises. Backwards generation squeezes everything to fit the label, leaving artificial patterns. Real data doesn't come from labels; labels describe data that already exists.
931.po: Models trained on naturally-ordered synthetic data stayed much closer to real performance (accuracy drops of 4.9% to 13.7%), while backwards-ordered data caused massive drops (up to 59.1%), showing the direction of generation matters significantly for training quality.

932.bp: Fact-checkers need to verify claims by looking up evidence, and large language models can help do this automatically by searching for relevant information and deciding if a claim is true or false. This matters for fighting misinformation at scale.
932.wh: Language models have a deep problem: they have their own internal knowledge from training, and sometimes that knowledge is wrong. When you fetch external evidence that contradicts what the model 'knows,' the model may ignore the evidence and stick with its incorrect belief—especially if it's confident. Standard fact-checking systems don't handle this collision between internal and external knowledge.
932.ap: This paper introduces KnowFC, which recognizes that language models need to distinguish what they actually know from what they don't know. The system uses reinforcement learning to teach the model to be honest about its knowledge gaps (inspired by the Dunning-Kruger effect, where overconfident people don't know what they're missing). When checking facts, the system retrieves evidence more carefully based on where the model's knowledge boundaries are, then builds a reasoning graph from evidence and uses math from causal analysis to block the model's internal knowledge from interfering with the verification.
932.ww: By making the model aware of its own knowledge boundaries, it stops confidently asserting wrong things and becomes more willing to trust external evidence. The causal math removes the hidden influence of the model's pre-existing beliefs, so the model judges the evidence fairly rather than filtering it through what it already thought.
932.po: The framework navigates the conflict between internal knowledge and external evidence more reliably than prior fact-checking systems, improving correctness and reducing cases where the model confidently states false things based on outdated internal knowledge.

933.bp: Knowledge graphs—structured databases of facts like 'Albert Einstein discovered relativity'—help companies organize information for search, recommendation, and decision-making. To apply causal reasoning (figuring out if X causes Y) over these graphs, you need to know the true effect of each action.
933.wh: Knowledge graphs have two problems that break traditional causal methods. First, many attribute values are missing (the 'open-world' assumption: just because you don't see a fact doesn't mean it's false). Second, entities aren't independent—changing one person's age affects recommendations to their friends, creating spillover effects that simple causal math ignores. Existing methods assume you have complete data or pretend entities don't interact.
933.ap: BaLu reformulates the problem as two connected prediction tasks using graph neural networks. First, it fills in missing attributes by learning patterns from the rest of the graph (predicting which entities connect to which attributes). Second, it estimates causal effects by treating the entities and their relationships as a network where information flows through connections, capturing how one entity's treatment affects neighbors.
933.ww: Graph neural networks learn by passing information between connected nodes, so they naturally capture how entities influence each other—the spillover effect. By training both tasks together, the system learns attribute patterns and causal patterns in one go. This way, filling in missing data and estimating effects reinforce each other.
933.po: BaLu outperforms existing methods on benchmark datasets, even when those baselines use powerful separate attribute-filling techniques, showing that joint learning handles incomplete and interconnected knowledge graphs better.

934.bp: Phishing websites fool people into giving away passwords and personal information by impersonating legitimate sites. Detecting these fraudulent domains protects billions of users from theft and fraud.
934.wh: Phishing sites are designed to look and feel like real sites, so surface-level tricks don't work well. Traditional machine learning looks at features of the domain name and HTML structure, but clever attackers constantly evolve their tactics to bypass old detection rules.
934.ap: U-Proof tests two approaches side by side: large language models and traditional machine learning algorithms. The system ingests a mix of real phishing websites from September 2024, along with genuine banking and postal service URLs, and evaluates how well each model type spots phishing. The tool also generates explanations showing what red flags each model saw, to help users understand the attack.
934.ww: Large language models can understand semantic meaning and contextual clues (e.g., subtle wording that mimics but doesn't exactly match a real bank). Traditional ML picks up on structural patterns in domains and code. Testing both gives you more signals and helps pick the best approach for this particular problem.
934.po: The paper compares LLM and traditional model performance on a custom dataset of recent phishing sites, offering a tool that combines both approaches for detection plus human-readable explanations to raise user awareness.

935.bp: Online recommendation systems need to suggest what item a user will want to interact with next based on their past history. Getting this right means more engagement and user satisfaction across platforms like Netflix, Spotify, and Amazon.
935.wh: Sequential recommendations are tricky because you need to track the order of past clicks and purchases—not just which items matter, but when they mattered. Most modern diffusion approaches squeeze all the history into a single summary, losing the rich temporal details. Meanwhile, explicit signals like 'user clicked item A right after item B' exist but are underused.
935.ap: DCRec uses diffusion models (systems that gradually add and remove noise to generate new sequences) with two types of conditions. Implicit conditions capture the overall summary of user behavior, and explicit conditions feed in user-item relationships and sequential patterns directly. The system embeds both types of conditions into the forward and reverse diffusion process (the phases where noise is added and removed), so neither signal gets lost.
935.ww: By carrying both implicit and explicit signals through the entire diffusion process, the model preserves the rich sequential structure while also respecting hard facts about user interactions. Using explicit patterns directly grounds the generation in observed reality, preventing the model from inventing implausible sequences.
935.po: The model generates more accurate next-item predictions by keeping both the overall behavior patterns and the specific sequential relationships intact, as shown in experiments on Amazon datasets.

936.bp: Causal learning—understanding which variables cause which outcomes—is becoming essential in healthcare, business, and policy. But researchers building new causal methods have no standard way to compare performance fairly, making it hard to know which method to trust.
936.wh: The causal learning field is growing fast with many new algorithms, but there's no agreed-upon collection of benchmark datasets, evaluation metrics, or protocols. Different researchers test on different data and report different metrics, so you can't tell if algorithm A is actually better than algorithm B or just was tested differently.
936.ap: CausalBench is a workshop and framework aimed at surveying existing benchmarking efforts, categorizing them by technical type, and identifying gaps. The workshop solicits papers on benchmark datasets, algorithms, models, and metrics for causal learning tasks like causal discovery (finding which variables cause which) and causal inference (estimating the size of causal effects).
936.ww: A shared benchmarking effort creates a level playing field. When everyone tests on the same datasets and reports the same metrics, you can genuinely compare algorithms and make faster progress. It also encourages reproducibility and forces researchers to think about bias and fairness from the start.
936.po: The workshop pushes the field toward standardized benchmarks, making it easier for users to pick the right causal method and for researchers to validate new algorithms objectively.

937.bp: Researchers need to find relevant papers to read, cite, and recommend. Program committees need reviewers who understand submissions. Funding agencies need peer reviewers. Better search and recommendation makes academic science more efficient.
937.wh: Academic papers live across many sources (arXiv, journals, conferences), each with different indexing and metadata. A single search API doesn't exist. Also, papers aren't just isolated documents—they're connected by citations and authorship, and different ranking methods (some neural, some linear algebra) capture different patterns.
937.ap: Scholar API (SAPI) provides a unified interface that talks to multiple data sources behind the scenes. Users can pick from four different ways to rank papers: Specter (deep learning on abstracts), ProNE-s (linear algebra on the citation graph), SciNCL (fine-tuned neural embeddings), and a graph neural network approach. The system federates requests across sources, letting researchers mash up recommendations creatively.
937.ww: Offering multiple ranking methods lets you experiment with combinations—e.g., finding papers that neural methods agree are relevant but linear-algebra methods also support, which might be more robust. A unified API with flexible backends means you don't rebuild the data pipeline each time someone has a new idea.
937.po: SAPI simplifies building academic search and recommendation tools by offering convenient access to multiple data sources and ranking methods through one interface, demonstrated through baseline implementations.

938.bp: When a model is trained to recognize people's faces in photos and write captions about them, it learns to associate faces with identities. If someone later asks the model to forget them (a right granted by privacy law), we need proof the model actually forgot, not just stopped mentioning their name.
938.wh: Current approaches to machine unlearning (removing a person's influence from a model) are hard to evaluate fairly. The same caption—'a woman smiling'—might be correct after unlearning or might be incorrect because the model is now hiding information it still actually knows. There's no standard way to measure whether the model truly forgot or is just being evasive.
938.ap: CelebCaption is a dataset of 15,000 photos of 150 famous people with four captions per photo—some detailed, some brief, and some with or without the person's name. This variation lets researchers test three things: whether the model stops using the name (Identity Removal), whether it stops relying on person-specific patterns (Specificity Reduction), and whether the captions are still good quality (Performance Preservation). The paper benchmarks existing unlearning methods against these three criteria.
938.ww: The varied captions isolate different aspects of what 'forgetting' means. A model that truly forgot won't use the name or person-specific details, but will still generate reasonable captions. A model that's just hiding information will fail one of these tests.
938.po: The benchmark shows that current unlearning methods fail to truly erase identity information from models—they either degrade caption quality or still leave hidden person-specific patterns—revealing the gap between current practice and real privacy.

939.bp: The web is built on graphs—hyperlinks connect pages, social networks connect people, knowledge bases connect facts. Understanding these graphs helps with search, misinformation detection, and building trustworthy online systems.
939.wh: Traditional graph algorithms don't explain why they made a decision, making them hard to trust. Large graphs change over time, requiring algorithms that adapt. And building one giant model for the entire web is impractical—you need methods that work across decentralized systems.
939.ap: WEB&GRAPH 2026 is a workshop bringing together researchers to discuss better graph algorithms, particularly focusing on interpretability, adaptation, and human-AI collaboration. Topics include detecting false information, tracking how information spreads, handling evolving networks, and building systems that explain their reasoning.
939.ww: By uniting web search, data mining, AI, and social science perspectives, the workshop creates space for methods that are both mathematically sound and socially aware—algorithms that work at scale but also explain themselves and respect human values.
939.po: The workshop aims to advance the field toward graph systems that are explainable, trustworthy, and aligned with human values, particularly for critical applications like misinformation detection and recommendation.

940.bp: Online stores often sell bundles—like 'video game + controller + game pass' or 'shampoo + conditioner + brush'—as a unit. Recommending bundles is different from recommending individual items because people care about the whole package together.
940.wh: Bundle recommendation has a tough problem: new bundles are created constantly and have no historical user interactions. Traditional methods can't recommend a bundle if nobody has ever rated it before. The old approaches also ignore that some items go well together—a controller matters more if you're buying a gaming console.
940.ap: EpicCBR uses graphs to connect items, bundles, and users, then applies contrastive learning (a method that pushes similar things close together and pulls different things apart). It identifies which items are central to user interests, builds profiles of users likely to want new bundles based on their past item preferences, and characterizes new bundles by looking at similar historical bundles and user preferences. A multi-view system handles both cold-start (new bundles) and warm-start (established bundles) scenarios.
940.ww: By thinking about item relationships and user preferences directly, rather than waiting for bundle interactions, the system can reason about new bundles. Using multiple views (user-item, bundle-item, historical patterns) means you have several signals to evaluate a new bundle, so you're not blindly guessing.
940.po: The method significantly outperforms prior bundle recommendation systems in cold-start scenarios (improvements up to 387%), allowing stores to recommend new packages immediately after they're created.

941.bp: Taxonomies organize concepts hierarchically—like 'Animal > Mammal > Dog'—and they're fundamental to search engines, e-commerce, and knowledge management. As the world changes, new entities (like 'cryptocurrency' or 'metaverse') need to be slotted into the right place.
941.wh: Picking the right parent-child relationship for a new entity requires understanding subtle semantic similarities. Existing approaches score each possible position with traditional contrastive learning, using negative examples that are randomly chosen. Random negatives are often too easy—the model solves the problem without learning anything useful. Cherry-picking hard negatives requires human judgment, which is impractical.
941.ap: TaxoDiff uses a diffusion model (a generative system) to create negative examples dynamically during training. At each training step, the system generates negative examples with varying difficulty—some easy to distinguish from the right answer, some harder. The diffusion process lets you control this hardness by sampling from different noise levels, automatically creating a curriculum of challenges.
941.ww: A curriculum of negative examples—starting easier, getting harder—helps a model learn robust features rather than overfitting to one particular type of wrong answer. The diffusion model's ability to generate examples on-the-fly means you adapt to what the model is struggling with, rather than guessing in advance what negatives to use.
941.po: The method achieves state-of-the-art taxonomy completion performance on three benchmarks by dynamically generating hard negatives throughout training, outperforming systems with fixed or random negative sampling.

942.bp: Recommendation systems predict what a user will want to watch or buy next based on their browsing and purchase history. Sequential context matters—someone who just searched for 'running shoes' is more likely to buy socks than someone browsing electronics.
942.wh: Diffusion models are good at generating diverse, realistic sequences, but existing diffusion recommendation methods have two problems: they lose stability when adding noise to the sequence (sample drift), and they don't handle real-world data well, which is often noisy and incomplete.
942.ap: GSDiffRec adds two specialized modules to diffusion-based recommendation. The Semantic-Targeted Guidance Module uses an enhanced transformer with special attention patterns and convolutional layers to understand user behavior more deeply. The Geodesic Diffusion Module adds geometric constraints during the noise-adding and noise-removal phases, keeping the generated sequence on a smooth manifold (a mathematical surface that respects the structure of real data).
942.ww: Geometric constraints during diffusion keep the generation process stable and grounded in realistic patterns, preventing the model from drifting into implausible sequences. The enhanced transformer captures semantic richness, so the guidance is actually meaningful rather than just steering randomly.
942.po: The method outperforms prior diffusion-based and traditional recommendation systems on Amazon datasets, with ablation studies showing both modules contribute meaningfully to performance.

943.bp: Social media shapes how people think, feel, and organize politically. Understanding the emotional dynamics—anger, joy, fear—helps explain why polarization spreads and how misinformation takes hold. Better understanding of emotion could inform better platform design.
943.wh: Research on social media has mostly focused on *what* people share (information flow) and *who* they connect to (network structure), but treated emotion as incidental. In reality, emotion is the driver—it determines what you pay attention to, who you trust, and how you respond.
943.ap: This talk uses natural language processing to measure emotions and moral sentiments in online text. It analyzes how emotions spread between people (emotional contagion), showing that exposure to others' emotions influences your own emotional expressions, beliefs, and sense of belonging. The research tracks emotional dynamics across political discourse, showing how in-group and out-group interactions differ emotionally.
943.ww: Emotions aren't just expressed; they're contagious and reshape entire populations' psychology. When you measure actual emotional patterns in posts (anger toward out-groups, joy in in-groups), you see the mechanism by which polarization becomes entrenched—it's not just disagreement, it's emotional organizing.
943.po: The evidence shows emotional dynamics underlie political polarization (characterized by in-group favoritism and out-group animosity) and collective social phenomena, revealing emotion as the hidden driver of social behavior that information-centric approaches miss.

944.bp: Doctors need to predict patient outcomes—readmission risk, length of stay, disease progression—to make better care decisions. Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich patient histories, but they're messy and incomplete, making it hard to use them directly for prediction.
944.wh: EHR data is enormous (many lab tests, diagnoses, medications), heterogeneous (numbers, dates, text), and sparse (not every patient has every test). Language models can help by using medical knowledge to fill gaps, but most prior work treats this as a general compression problem—the model cleans up the EHR without knowing what prediction task it's being cleaned for. This wastes information.
944.ap: ReToP (Rewrite-To-Predict) trains an LLM-based system end-to-end for a specific prediction task. It generates synthetic training examples using a clinician-driven feature selection strategy to show the model different ways to rewrite patient records. Importantly, it uses a novel scoring method (Classifier Supervised Contribution) that measures how much each rewritten record helps the downstream prediction model, so the rewrite process focuses on clinically relevant changes.
944.ww: By tuning the rewrite directly to the prediction task, the system learns which parts of the EHR matter for *that particular prediction*—e.g., lab values matter for sepsis prediction but maybe not for appointment no-show prediction. This task-aware approach generates rewrites that actually help predict, rather than generic cleaning.
944.po: ReToP outperforms baseline models on three clinical prediction tasks using MIMIC-IV data, showing that aligning EHR rewriting with the prediction goal improves performance.
